coverage_window.note: UK-focused run covering Friday 20 November and the night that followed. The window's defining item is not a UK incident but it lands squarely on UK government: VMware vCenter CVE-2026-123890 is confirmed exploited as a zero-day since early September by ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221), CISA added it to KEV on 20 November with a three-day deadline of 23 November, and NHS England Digital had already issued its own cyber alert CC-4899 on 19 November rating it High and citing observed in-the-wild exploitation. It takes rank 1 because it is not a patching job - BONESAW extracted the vmdir database and SAML STS signing material and created an SSO administrator account, so the correct response is a compromise hunt over ten weeks of history plus a decision about rotating signing material, and the reported intrusion reached vCenter through internal Linux appliances that had no EDR coverage. Rank 2 is Transport for London, retained from yesterday's rank 1 because the scope grew inside the window: around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers, revised up from 250,000, with TfL stating the investigation is incomplete and the figure may rise again; security question answers remain the part that cannot be rotated. Rank 3 is the rest of the 20 November KEV batch - Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448, Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 and SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-42884 - and contains the week's most dangerous false assurance: disabling XML-RPC in the Roller admin UI does NOT mitigate the flaw, because affected versions deserialise the request before checking the feature flag, and the same bug was patched in September under CVE-2026-82384 for 6.1.5 only. Rank 4 is the NCSC/Defra/FSA refrigeration operation, which has turned from a covert programme into an actionable advisory inside the window: Pen Test Partners independently verified the Omega Solutions finding, RDM has shipped initial security updates while still disputing severity, and the NCSC's advice to operators is explicit - patch, change default credentials, get the devices off the internet. Rank 5 is N-able, where a three-day 'platform configuration' explanation became a confirmed cyberattack on 18 November, and where a separate incident has N-central hosted platforms offline worldwide with on-premises customers told to keep servers shut down; organisations behind Mail Assure or SpamExperts have a 16-20 November email forensic gap. Rank 6 corrects and corroborates the FCA/PRA/BoE consultation date (19 November, GC26/9 / CP17/26, aligned to the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework, responses due 26 February 2027). Rank 7 holds NGINX2Root at yesterday's downgrade with the numbers that justify it: roughly 9 million exposed services per Censys, still no confirmed exploitation, still not in KEV - but the kernel SCTP flaw completing the chain to root has no CVE and no upstream patch, so blacklisting an unused module is the highest-value five-minute action in this report. Rank 8 is the European Commission's confirmation of an AI-assisted attack that took HR, medical reimbursement and translation systems offline for over ten days, detected 22 October and confirmed only on 19 November - included for the four-week attribution gap rather than the AI tooling. Rank 9 is the UK corporate board, deliberately low confidence: Aurora claims 1.1 TB from William Cook Holdings including payroll data, N0n published alleged Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan customer data from unnamed third parties while also carrying a documented record of fabricated listings, and The Gentlemen named Nvidia without evidence. Rank 10 is the deadline and patch-completeness board: Apache Axis, REDCap, LiteLLM and Synology deadlines fall today, Axis has no vendor fix at all, and four simultaneous incomplete-fix or reissued-identifier cases now mean a closed ticket and a clean identifier-matching scan are no longer evidence that a bug is closed. Eight entries are new or materially updated. Rotated out from yesterday: the Drupal installer RCE (no new information in the window; the install.php deny rule is carried into rank 7's change ticket), the FastUnlock Windows 11 lock-screen zero-day (no new information), the UK military cyber force disclosure (retained as context in rank 4) and the OPTIMJACK / HSBC CSP finding (rotated into rank 9's supplier theme). Also considered and not ranked: the Chaos ransomware affiliate arrests in Ukraine (Europol-coordinated, no NCA involvement established), the Gibraltar government cloud intrusion (no update since 9-11 November), the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill's position at Commons consideration of Lords amendments (no November date confirmed) and the Bristol schools and 3AM school estate incidents (early November, no new information).

vulnerabilities.title: VMware vCenter CVE-2026-123890 Confirmed Exploited as a Zero-Day Since Early September by ARMORY CASTLE (ex-UNC5221) - Added to CISA KEV on 20 November with a 23 November Deadline, and NHS England Digital Has Issued Its Own Cyber Alert CC-4899
affected_products: VMware vCenter Server 8.0 - patched 19 November 2026 under VMSA-2026-0009
VMware vCenter Server 7.0 - reached end of general support in October 2025; at least one report states no public patch is available for this branch
vCenter components bundled in VMware Cloud Foundation
vCenter components bundled in VMware vSphere Foundation
vCenter components bundled in VMware Telco Cloud products
Same advisory (VMSA-2026-0009) also fixes four further issues in VMware SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows
Vulnerable component: VMware Directory Service (vmdir) - authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel
vulnerabilities.summary:
This is the most consequential item in the window and it is not a patching job. It is a compromise hunt with a three-day federal deadline attached, and the UK government hook is already in place: NHS England Digital published its own cyber alert, CC-4899, on 19 November at 16:29, rating the threat severity High and stating that security researchers have observed exploitation in the wild.

The mechanism. CVE-2026-123890 is a critical authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service, the component that underpins vCenter Single Sign-On. It is classed as authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel, carries CVSS 9.8, and is reachable by a remote, unauthenticated attacker who can obtain an administrator session on vCenter Server. Broadcom shipped the fix on 19 November 2026 in VMSA-2026-0009, alongside four other issues in SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows. Reporting states there is no workaround.

What makes this different from a normal critical CVE. Broadcom's advisory credits Mandiant with reporting the flaw but, according to multiple outlets, does not mention that it was already being exploited. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant published separately and attribute the activity to ARMORY CASTLE, formerly tracked as UNC5221 and also referenced as Warp Panda, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor. Exploitation began in early September 2026 - more than two months before a fix existed. Mandiant further reports evidence that the group knew of the flaw before 29 July, the date CVE-2026-59309, a separate vCenter authentication bypass, was disclosed. The practical consequence: if you run vCenter 7.x or 8.x and it was reachable from anywhere an attacker had a foothold, the question for this week is not whether you are patched. It is whether you were already compromised between early September and 19 November, and patching does not answer that question.

The attack chain, which is the part worth reading twice. In the intrusion Mandiant describes, initial access did not come through vCenter at all - it came through a separate BeyondTrust zero-day, CVE-2026-102764, after which the actor moved laterally to internal Linux appliances that lacked EDR coverage. Against vCenter the group used BONESAW, a custom Go utility with a build timestamp of 13 July 2026, capable of fully compromising vCenter 7.x and 8.x appliances. BONESAW was observed extracting /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb - the vmdir database - obtaining SAML Security Token Service signing material, and creating an SSO administrator account. Possession of STS signing material is the detail that should set the severity of your response: an attacker who can sign their own SAML assertions can mint authenticated sessions across everything that trusts that identity provider, and rotating a password does not revoke that. Reconnaissance preceding exploitation used nmap against ports associated with vCenter and adjacent services, including 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080. Follow-on tooling observed in successful intrusions includes SAWSNAKE, BEARBONES, LAZYBONES, SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH. Google has published YARA rules for all six families along with detection coverage in Google Security Operations.

Why the UK public sector should treat this as a priority over the weekend. vCenter is the management plane for a very large share of UK government, NHS trust, local authority and university virtualisation estates, and it is frequently reachable from the internal corporate network rather than isolated on an out-of-band management segment. The three elements combine badly: a management-plane authentication bypass, an espionage actor with two and a half months of undetected access, and a reported initial-access route through appliances that were outside EDR coverage. The appliance-with-no-EDR problem is the one most UK estates share. Note also the vCenter 7.0 position - end of general support since October 2025, with at least one report stating no public patch is available - which for anyone still on that branch converts this from a patch into a migration or an isolation decision taken this week.

CISA added CVE-2026-123890 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 20 November 2026, in the same batch as Apache Roller, Cisco Expressway and SAP NetWeaver (rank 3), with a remediation deadline of 23 November 2026 under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. A three-day deadline is itself a signal about CISA's confidence in the exploitation evidence. UK bodies are not bound by BOD 26-04, but the deadline is a reasonable proxy for how fast the US government believes this needs to move.

Confidence and caveats. Confidence is high on the identifier, the CVSS score, the vmdir component, the 19 November patch date and advisory number, the KEV addition on 20 November, the ARMORY CASTLE attribution and the BONESAW tradecraft - these are consistent across SecurityWeek, Help Net Security, BleepingComputer, SOC Prime, Cyber Kendra and the Google Cloud threat intelligence blog listing. The NHS England Digital alert CC-4899 is evidenced by its title, publication timestamp and severity rating as surfaced through search; the alert body was not retrieved because all direct page fetches failed in this run. The Google/Mandiant IOC tables, file hashes and YARA rule contents were NOT retrieved - only the behavioural indicators and family names are recorded below, and you should pull the full indicator set from the Mandiant blog directly. The number of compromised organisations has not been stated publicly. The vCenter 7.0 no-patch claim is single-source and should be checked against Broadcom's advisory matrix before you act on it.
recommended_actions: Patch vCenter to the VMSA-2026-0009 fixed releases as an emergency change, not a scheduled one. CISA's deadline for US federal bodies is 23 November. If you are on the 7.0 branch, verify Broadcom's advisory matrix directly - one report states no public patch is available for that end-of-general-support branch, which makes isolation or migration the decision instead.

Then treat the estate as potentially compromised since early September and run a hunt, because patching does not evict an actor who has already been inside for ten weeks. Scope the hunt to vCenter, ESXi and the adjacent Linux appliances, not vCenter alone.

Enumerate every vCenter SSO administrator account and compare against your change records. BONESAW was observed creating an SSO administrator account; an account you cannot tie to an approved change is an incident, not a finding.

Assume SAML Security Token Service signing material is compromised on any host you cannot clear, and rotate it. An attacker holding STS signing keys can mint valid assertions for every service that trusts that identity provider, and a password reset does not revoke that capability. Rotating signing material is disruptive, which is exactly why it needs deciding this week rather than discovering later.
Check for access to /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb and for any copy of that file outside its normal path. Exfiltration of the vmdir database is the observed objective.

Pull the full indicator set and YARA rules from the Google Cloud / Mandiant ARMORY CASTLE publication and load the rules for BONESAW, SAWSNAKE, BEARBONES, LAZYBONES, SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH. The indicators below are behavioural only; the hashes were not retrieved in this run.

Close the gap the attack chain actually used: inventory every appliance - virtualisation, backup, identity, remote access, refrigeration, anything shipped as a sealed Linux image - and record whether it carries EDR. The reported intrusion moved laterally through internal Linux appliances that had no EDR coverage. That inventory is worth more than this single patch.

Check your BeyondTrust estate against CVE-2026-102764, the reported initial-access leg. This feed recorded a vendor/product dispute on that identifier on 17 October; resolve the dispute against the vendor advisory rather than against a scanner's product string.

Remove vCenter, ESXi and SDDC Manager management interfaces from any network segment reachable by ordinary user endpoints, and verify by scanning from a user VLAN rather than by reading the firewall policy.

NHS organisations: action CC-4899 through your normal cyber alert process and record the response. The alert is dated 19 November with a High severity rating and explicitly references observed in-the-wild exploitation.

kql.name: vCenter SSO administrator account creation - ARMORY CASTLE / BONESAW
kql.description: Primary detection. BONESAW was observed creating an SSO administrator account on compromised vCenter appliances. Any such creation outside an approved change is an incident. Requires vCenter appliance syslog forwarding.
kql.query:
let lookback = 120d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Computer has_any ("vcenter", "vcsa", "vsphere")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("vmdird", "vmdir", "sso", "vmware-sts", "vmafd")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("Add entry", "CreateUser", "user created", "added to group", "Administrators@vsphere.local", "member add")
| extend Principal = extract(@"(?:cn=|user[ =:])([A-Za-z0-9._\\-]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SeverityLevel, Principal, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Access to or copy of the vmdir database file data.mdb
kql.description: BONESAW extracted /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb to obtain directory contents and SAML STS signing material. Any read, copy or archive of that path by a process other than vmdird is suspicious.
kql.query:
let lookback = 120d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where SyslogMessage has "data.mdb" or SyslogMessage has "vmware-vmdir"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("cp ", "tar", "scp", "curl", "wget", "gzip", "base64", "dd if=", "cat ")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Reconnaissance against the vCenter management port set (443, 2012, 5480, 9080)
kql.description: ARMORY CASTLE conducted nmap reconnaissance against ports associated with vCenter and related services before exploitation. Distinct-port fan-out from a single internal source is the signal, not the individual connection.
kql.query:
let lookback = 120d;
let vcPorts = dynamic([443, 2012, 5480, 9080, 8089, 7444]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DestinationPort in (vcPorts)
| summarize DistinctPorts = dcount(DestinationPort), PortList = make_set(DestinationPort, 10), DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), Attempts = count()
    by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctPorts >= 3 or DistinctTargets >= 5
| order by Attempts desc

kql.name: Unexpected SAML assertion issuance after suspected STS signing material theft
kql.description: If STS signing material was stolen, the attacker can mint valid assertions. Hunt for federated sign-ins that do not correspond to a known device or location. Tune heavily - this is a hunting query, not a rule.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where AuthenticationProtocol has_any ("saml", "wsFederation")
| extend Dev = tostring(DeviceDetail.deviceId), Loc = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize SignIns = count(), Countries = make_set(Loc, 10), Devices = dcount(Dev) by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName
| where Devices == 0 or array_length(Countries) > 2
| order by SignIns desc

kql.name: Go binaries and archive staging on virtualisation management hosts
kql.description: BONESAW is a Go utility (build timestamp 13 July 2026). Hunt for unexpected statically linked binaries and staging activity on or adjacent to virtualisation management infrastructure.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceName has_any ("vcenter", "vcsa", "esxi", "vsphere", "sddc")
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/", "/var/tmp/", "/dev/shm/")
| where FileName in~ ("tar", "gzip", "zip", "base64", "openssl", "curl", "wget", "nc", "socat")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("data.mdb", "vmware-vmdir", "/storage/db/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Outbound connections from virtualisation appliances
kql.description: Appliances should not initiate arbitrary outbound connections. This query surfaces egress from management-plane hosts, which is where the EDR coverage gap in the reported intrusion would have shown.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceName has_any ("vcenter", "vcsa", "esxi", "vsphere", "sddc", "nsx")
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| order by Connections desc

vulnerabilities.title: UK Government: Transport for London Revised the Oyster Photocard Breach Up to Around 265,000 Customers and Says the Figure May Rise Again - Security Question Answers Are in Scope, the ICO Is Notified, and the Entry Point Is Still Undisclosed
affected_products: TfL Oyster photocard website and account platform (taken offline; restoration date not announced)
Affected card types include Zip photocards for children and young people, 18+ Student Oyster, Apprentice Oyster, Care Leaver Oyster, 60+ London Oyster and Veterans Oyster
Approximately 265,000 photocard customers, revised up from an earlier estimate of around 250,000; TfL says the investigation is incomplete and the figure may increase further
vulnerabilities.summary:
Carried forward from yesterday at rank 1 and retained at rank 2 because the window contains a material change: the number of affected customers has been revised upward from around 250,000 to around 265,000, and TfL says the investigation is not complete and the figure may increase again. A breach whose scope is still growing five days after detection is not a closed incident, and the coverage dated 20 November - Help Net Security and Computer Weekly among them - is the first reporting to carry the revised number.

What happened, restated for completeness. TfL detected the compromise on 16 November when existing customers began receiving account-creation emails they had not requested. That is the detail worth dwelling on: the attacker drove a legitimate TfL workflow at scale from inside TfL's own platform, and the detection path was customer complaint, not telemetry. TfL took the Oyster photocard website offline, notified customers on 18 November, notified the Information Commissioner's Office, and the story broke publicly on 19 November. The entry point remains undisclosed, and no actor has been named.

The data. Reporting differs on the exact field list and that difference matters, so both versions are recorded. The narrower account is full names, phone numbers and email addresses. The broader and more commonly reported account is names, email addresses, home addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and security questions together with their answers. TfL's own position is consistent across outlets on what was NOT taken: passwords, bank and payment details, and journey data were not compromised, and photographs were not exposed. Oyster photocards continue to work.

Why the security answers are the whole story. Passwords get rotated and the exposure ends. A date of birth, a home address and the answer to a static security question cannot be rotated, and they are precisely the three things UK call centres - at TfL and at every bank, utility, local authority and NHS trust those same Londoners deal with - accept as telephone identity proof. The consequence of TfL's loss therefore lands on organisations that had nothing to do with it. TfL's remediation is correct as far as it goes: once the portal is restored, all photocard customers will be prompted to change their password, security question and answer. But it only protects TfL.

The second-order exposure is the card types. The affected products are not generic travel accounts; they disclose status. A Zip photocard identifies a child, an 18+ Student Oyster identifies a student, an Apprentice Oyster identifies an apprentice, a Care Leaver Oyster identifies a care leaver and a Veterans Oyster identifies a veteran. A dataset that pairs a name, home address, date of birth and 'is a care leaver' or 'is a child' is materially more useful for targeted social engineering than a dataset of 265,000 generic customer records, and the London Assembly has published its own statement on the exposure.

Regulatory context. TfL reported the incident to the ICO and says it has found no evidence that the compromised data has been used. Whether the ICO opens a formal investigation is not yet known; one outlet notes it is unclear whether the ICO will investigate or take action. The relevant precedent is TfL's own 2024 cyber attack, after which the ICO investigated and chose not to take enforcement action, having judged TfL's response proportionate. No compensation scheme has been announced, and the ICO cannot award compensation in any event.

Confidence and caveats. Confidence is high on the 16 November detection date, the website being taken offline, the 18 November customer notification, the ICO notification, the revised figure of approximately 265,000 and TfL's statement that the figure may rise - these are consistent across BleepingComputer, Computer Weekly, ITPro, The Register, Help Net Security and Neowin. The exact exposed field list is reported inconsistently between outlets and both versions are recorded above. The attacker's entry point, the actor identity and the restoration date are all undisclosed. No TfL or ICO primary page was retrieved in this run because all direct page fetches failed.
recommended_actions: If you have not already done it after yesterday's report: put a rate alert on your own transactional email volume today. TfL's compromise surfaced because customers received account-creation emails they had not asked for, generated by the attacker driving a legitimate workflow inside TfL's own platform. If your platform can send a large volume of account emails without anything internal flagging it, you have the same gap, and closing it is a configuration change rather than a project.

Stop accepting static security answers, dates of birth and home addresses as telephone identity proof. Around 265,000 Londoners' answers are now in circulation and cannot be rotated. This is the control that protects your organisation from someone else's breach, and the TfL dataset is a good enough reason to make the change this quarter.

Treat any inbound contact referencing a London travel concession - Zip, 18+ Student, Apprentice, Care Leaver, 60+ or Veterans Oyster - as a fraud indicator in your contact-centre scripts for the next several months. The card types disclose age, student, apprentice, care-leaver and veteran status, which is what makes this dataset useful for targeted approaches.

If you are a local authority, NHS trust, school, college or charity serving London: expect your service users to be in this dataset and brief frontline staff accordingly. Your organisation can be defrauded using data TfL lost.

Monitor account-creation and password-reset workflows for volume anomalies as a standing control, not a one-off check, and alert on the ratio of account-creation emails to actual completed registrations. A high send volume with a low completion rate is the signature of what happened here.

Re-read your own breach detection assumptions against this case. The detection path was a customer complaint. Ask honestly which of your own platforms would surface this class of abuse from telemetry alone, and write the answer down.

Where you hold static security answers, plan their removal. Replace them with one-time codes to a verified channel or with knowledge the organisation can itself invalidate. Static answers are a liability whose exposure you cannot remediate.
Do not treat the 265,000 figure as final. TfL has stated the investigation is incomplete and the number may increase. If you are tracking exposure for your own service users, revisit it.

kql.name: Account creation volume anomaly - the TfL detection gap
kql.description: The cheapest control in this report. Alerts when account-creation events in an hour exceed a multiple of the rolling baseline. TfL's attacker generated account emails at scale and nothing internal flagged it.
kql.query:
let baselineWindow = 30d;
let detectWindow = 7d;
let creations = AuditLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(baselineWindow)
    | where OperationName has_any ("Add user", "Create user", "Invite external user", "Register user")
    | summarize Creations = count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h);
let stats = creations | where TimeGenerated < ago(detectWindow) | summarize Avg = avg(Creations), Sd = stdev(Creations);
creations
| where TimeGenerated > ago(detectWindow)
| extend Avg = toscalar(stats | project Avg), Sd = toscalar(stats | project Sd)
| extend Threshold = Avg + (3 * Sd)
| where Creations > Threshold and Creations > 20
| project TimeGenerated, Creations, Avg = round(Avg, 1), Threshold = round(Threshold, 1)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Credential-stuffing pattern against customer-facing authentication
kql.description: Security answers, dates of birth and addresses from this breach feed account-recovery abuse elsewhere. Surfaces single sources attempting many distinct accounts.
kql.query:
let lookback = 14d;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ResultType != 0
| summarize DistinctAccounts = dcount(UserPrincipalName), Attempts = count(), Failures = make_set(ResultDescription, 5)
    by IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctAccounts >= 15
| order by DistinctAccounts desc

kql.name: Password and security-answer reset spikes per actor
kql.description: Detects an identity or service principal driving reset or recovery workflows at scale, the pattern reported inside TfL's platform.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where OperationName has_any ("Reset password", "Change password", "Update user", "Reset user password", "Self-service password reset")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), App = tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)
| summarize Operations = count(), Targets = dcount(tostring(TargetResources[0].id)) by coalesce(Actor, App), bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Operations > 25 or Targets > 25
| order by Operations desc

kql.name: Phishing referencing TfL, Oyster or London travel concessions
kql.description: Follow-on fraud against a dataset containing names, addresses, dates of birth and concession status. Tune the sender allowlist to your own legitimate TfL correspondence.

vulnerabilities.title: CISA Added Four Exploited Flaws to KEV on 20 November With a Three-Day Deadline of 23 November: Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448 (Pre-Auth XML-RPC RCE, Now Confirmed Exploited and Disabling XML-RPC Does NOT Mitigate It), Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 (Hard-Coded Erlang Cluster Cookie, Root) and SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-42884
affected_products: Apache Roller 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 - unauthenticated deserialization via /roller-services/xmlrpc; fixed in 6.1.6 (some sources say 6.1.7); the earlier 6.1.5 release fixed only the CVE-2026-82384 identifier for the same underlying bug

Cisco Expressway-C (Core) and Expressway-E (Edge), virtual and appliance, clustered deployments - advisory cisco-sa-vcs-static-cred-hr7EWZ8t; affected clusters reported as X15.5.3 and earlier; fixed in X15.5.20
SAP NetWeaver 7.50 - improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic; fix delivered via SAP Note 3660969
Fourth member of the same KEV batch: VMware vCenter CVE-2026-123890 - see rank 1
vulnerabilities.summary:
CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 20 November 2026 and set a single remediation deadline of 23 November 2026 under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. Three days is unusually short and is itself the finding: it indicates CISA is confident in the exploitation evidence for all four. The fourth member of the batch is the VMware vCenter zero-day at rank 1; the other three are bundled here.

Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448 - the one with the trap in it. CVSS 9.8, published 17 November 2026, deserialization of untrusted data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4, allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. The mechanism is an unauthenticated POST to /roller-services/xmlrpc carrying an ex:serializable Java object, which the server deserialises before any authentication or feature check. Apache has acknowledged that the issue is being actively exploited but has not published payload details, attribution or the stages of successful exploitation.

Two things about this one will catch people out. First, it is the same underlying bug as CVE-2026-82384, which was patched in September for 6.1.5 only - so an organisation that patched in September against the old identifier may still be exposed, and an identifier-matching scanner will agree with the September remediation record. This feed flagged exactly this pattern yesterday in the PHP advisory (rank 9 today) and the week before in the Zyxel wrong-KEV-CVE case. That is now four reissued-or-incomplete-fix cases in three weeks, and it is the single most important governance finding in this feed: a closed remediation ticket is no longer evidence that the bug is closed. Second, and worse: disabling XML-RPC in the Roller admin interface is NOT a mitigation. Apache states that affected versions deserialise the request before checking whether the XML-RPC feature is enabled. Anyone who 'mitigated' by turning the feature off in the UI has not mitigated anything. The real workarounds, if you cannot upgrade immediately, are to set enabledForExtensions to false in WEB-INF/web.xml, or to remove the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping, then restart Roller. The fix is 6.1.6 or later.

Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 - hard-coded credentials, root, no workaround. CVSS 9.8, CWE-798, covered by Cisco advisory cisco-sa-vcs-static-cred-hr7EWZ8t published 21 October 2026, affecting Expressway-C and Expressway-E in both virtual and appliance form. The flaw lives in the cluster database service, which runs on Erlang and listens on TCP 4372. A maintenance node identity - reported as 'wombat@' - and a matching Erlang cookie are compiled into the software, meaning they are identical on every installation. An unauthenticated attacker with network access to that port on a clustered device can execute OS commands as root. Cisco's position is that an attacker must possess the cookie; since the cookie ships in the binary, that is not a meaningful barrier, and Cisco lists no workaround. Fix is X15.5.20. Two further details matter: reporting indicates X15.5.20 does NOT close PHP2Shell, so plan a second hop to 15.5.21 or later rather than treating X15.5.20 as done; and one report describes an attacker using public exploit code to obtain root on four clustered gateways at a Russian organisation. Cisco's PSIRT was not aware of exploitation as at 21 October - the KEV addition on 20 November is the change.

SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-42884. Listed in KEV as improper neutralisation of special elements in data query logic. Reporting cites SAP NetWeaver 7.50 as affected and SAP Note 3660969 as the fix. This is the thinnest of the three in open reporting - note the 2025 identifier year, which means it has been available for exploitation for some time - and it needs checking against the SAP Security Patch Day notes rather than against secondary coverage.

UK relevance. Expressway is the edge component of Cisco Unified Communications and is common in NHS trusts, local authorities and universities for external video and mobile-and-remote-access collaboration - it is by design internet-facing, which is the worst possible pairing with a hard-coded root credential. Apache Roller is a smaller UK footprint but appears in university and research-institute blog estates. SAP NetWeaver sits under finance and HR systems in central government and large UK corporates, where patch windows are long and change control is heavy, so the 23 November deadline will not be met by most and the compensating control - restricting network reachability - matters more than the patch date.

Confidence and caveats. Confidence is high on the 20 November KEV addition of all four, the 23 November deadline, the Apache Roller mechanism and affected range, the fact that disabling XML-RPC is not a mitigation, and the Cisco Expressway hard-coded-cookie mechanism and TCP 4372 port - these are corroborated across The Hacker News, securityonline.info, SOC Prime, Corgea, Phoenix Security, OpenCVE and the KEV catalogue listing surfaced via an aggregated feed. CISA's own catalogue pages could not be fetched in this run. Sources disagree on the Roller fixed version (6.1.5 versus 6.1.6 versus 6.1.7) and at least one source states CVE-2026-129448 is not in KEV, which is contradicted by the 20 November listing. The Cisco exploitation report involving four gateways at a Russian organisation is single-source and unverified. The SAP NetWeaver details are secondary-source only.
recommended_actions: Apache Roller: upgrade to 6.1.6 or later. Do NOT rely on disabling XML-RPC in the admin interface - affected versions deserialise the request before checking whether the feature is enabled, so that control does nothing.

Apache Roller, if you cannot upgrade today: set enabledForExtensions to false in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping, then restart Roller. Block POST requests to /roller-services/xmlrpc at the reverse proxy or WAF as well, and leave the block in place after patching.

Apache Roller: specifically re-check any host you patched in September against CVE-2026-82384. That release line fixed 6.1.5 only; the same bug is now CVE-2026-129448 and is confirmed exploited. A closed September ticket is not evidence of safety here, and an identifier-matching scanner will not tell you otherwise.

Apache Roller: hunt retrospectively for POSTs to /roller-services/xmlrpc containing ex:serializable, and for any process spawned by the Roller servlet container. Exploitation is confirmed, so the correct assumption for an internet-facing instance is that it was attempted.
Cisco Expressway: upgrade clustered deployments to X15.5.20. There is no workaround. Then plan the second hop to 15.5.21 or later, because reporting indicates X15.5.20 does not close PHP2Shell.

Cisco Expressway, as the immediate compensating control: block TCP 4372 at the network boundary and restrict it to the cluster peers only. The hard-coded Erlang cookie is identical on every install, so reachability of that port is the whole exposure.
Cisco Expressway: hunt for unexpected root-level command execution and for Erlang distribution connections from non-peer addresses, and verify the cluster peer list against your own records.

SAP NetWeaver: apply SAP Note 3660969 and verify the note against the SAP Security Patch Day listing rather than against press coverage, which is thin on this one. Note the 2025 identifier - this has been exploitable for longer than the KEV date suggests.

SAP NetWeaver, where the change window is weeks away: restrict network reachability of the affected NetWeaver interfaces to known application and integration sources as the interim control, and record the risk acceptance with a date.

Treat 23 November as the planning date for all four, including vCenter at rank 1. UK bodies are not bound by BOD 26-04, but a three-day CISA deadline is a reasonable proxy for confidence in the exploitation evidence.

kql.name: Apache Roller XML-RPC deserialization attempts - CVE-2026-129448
kql.description: Primary detection. Any POST to /roller-services/xmlrpc from an untrusted source is suspicious; one carrying ex:serializable is an exploitation attempt. Substitute your reverse-proxy or Apache access-log table as appropriate.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriStem has "/roller-services/xmlrpc"
| extend Suspicious = iff(csUriQuery has_any ("serializable", "ex:serializable") or csMethod == "POST", true, false)
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, Suspicious
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Process execution spawned by the Roller servlet container
kql.description: Deserialization RCE manifests as the Java process spawning a shell. Any child process of the Roller/Tomcat user is an incident on a blog platform.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("tomcat", "roller", "catalina")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/bin/sh", "/bin/bash", "curl ", "wget ", "python", "perl", "nc ", "base64 -d", "chmod +x")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Cisco Expressway Erlang cluster port 4372 reachable from non-peer addresses
kql.description: The entire exposure for CVE-2026-76466 is reachability of TCP 4372, because the Erlang cookie is compiled into the software. Replace the peer list with your own cluster members.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
let clusterPeers = dynamic(["10.0.0.0", "10.0.0.1"]);  // replace with your Expressway cluster peer addresses
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DestinationPort == 4372
| where SourceIP !in (clusterPeers)
| summarize Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Targets = make_set(DestinationIP, 10)
    by SourceIP
| order by Attempts desc

kql.name: Root command execution on Cisco Expressway nodes
kql.description: Successful exploitation yields OS command execution as root via the cluster database service. Hunt for root-level activity not tied to an approved maintenance window.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Computer has_any ("expressway", "vcs", "expwy")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("root", "sudo", "su -", "erl_child_setup", "beam.smp")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/bin/sh", "/bin/bash", "curl", "wget", "useradd", "ssh-keygen", "authorized_keys", "crontab")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: SAP NetWeaver query-logic injection indicators - CVE-2025-42884
kql.description: Hunting starting point only; the public detail on this CVE is thin. Surfaces anomalous request patterns against NetWeaver application paths. Tune against your own integration sources.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DestinationPort in (8000, 8001, 44300, 50000, 50001)
| where RequestURL has_any ("/sap/bc/", "/sap/public/", "/irj/", "/webdynpro/")
| where RequestURL has_any ("'", "--", "%27", "UNION", "union", "SELECT", "select ", "..%2f")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Outbound egress from collaboration and blog platform hosts
kql.description: Post-exploitation callback detection across all three products in this bundle. Expressway, Roller and NetWeaver hosts should have narrow, known egress.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceName has_any ("expressway", "vcs", "roller", "netweaver", "sapnw")
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess" and RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 10), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| order by Connections desc

vulnerabilities.title: UK Government: the NCSC, Defra and Food Standards Agency Refrigeration Operation Is Now Public in Detail - Pen Test Partners Verified and Expanded the Finding, RDM Has Shipped Initial Security Updates While Disputing the Severity, and the NCSC's Advice to Operators Is Patch, Change Default Credentials, Get Off the Internet
affected_products: Resource Data Management refrigeration controllers (Intuitive / Data Manager family as deployed in commercial refrigeration) - no CVE identifier assigned
Thousands of controllers governing tens of thousands of commercial refrigeration units across the UK, per government and press accounts
Comparable class of weak-credential flaw previously abused against Danfoss refrigeration controllers in Europe
Out of scope of the government programme: convenience retail, wholesale, hospitality, catering, pharmacy and vaccine cold chain, and food manufacturing
vulnerabilities.summary:
Yesterday this was a story about a covert government operation. Today it is an actionable advisory, and the actionable parts arrived inside this window: a named independent verifier, vendor patches, and - for the first time - concrete NCSC guidance addressed to the operators who were never in the programme.

What is now established. A weak-password flaw in Resource Data Management refrigeration controllers was first uncovered in late October by staff at refrigeration consultancy Omega Solutions. Pen Test Partners subsequently verified and expanded on the findings, with Ken Munro linking it to the same weak-password class previously abused against Danfoss equipment in Europe. The NCSC, Defra and the Food Standards Agency coordinated an industry-wide response over roughly three weeks from late October: industry briefings, direct contact with affected businesses, and a coordinated disconnection and patching programme. Thousands of controllers governing tens of thousands of refrigeration units were taken off the open internet, and staff at some sites reverted to manual temperature monitoring - unplugging network cables and checking fridge temperatures by hand. No supermarket has been named in any reporting.

What is new today and changes what you should do. First, independent verification: Pen Test Partners is a named, credible third party, which moves the technical claim out of 'one consultancy reported it and the vendor disagrees' territory. Second, there is now something to install - RDM has released initial security updates and continues to work with the NCSC. 'Initial' is the operative word and is why patch_available is recorded as partial. Third, the NCSC's advice to operators is explicit and simple: apply the vendor's security updates, change default credentials, and keep the devices off the public internet. Fourth, Pen Test Partners assesses that the issue has been largely mitigated for the organisations inside the programme, while smaller businesses operating refrigeration equipment could still be exposed.

The disagreement, recorded rather than resolved. RDM says it has seen no sign of malicious activity and disputes the severity of the findings. The government judged the risk serious enough to run a three-week national disconnection programme with two departments and the FSA involved. Both positions are recorded because they are both on the record; an operator does not have to resolve them, because the remediation advice is identical under either reading. Changing a default password and taking an industrial controller off the public internet are correct regardless of whose severity assessment is right, and neither costs anything.

Who is still exposed, and why they do not know it. The programme reached the major grocers. It did not reach convenience retail, wholesale, hospitality, catering, pharmacy and vaccine cold chain, or food manufacturing. The structural reason those operators cannot answer the exposure question from their own records is that a refrigeration contractor commissioned the equipment, often with a remote-monitoring connection as a service feature, and the device never entered the IT asset inventory. There is no asset register entry, no change record, and frequently no awareness that the fridge has an IP address at all. This is the same pattern as building management systems, CCTV and door controllers, and it is why the recommended action below is a written question to the contractor plus an external scan of your own address space, rather than a database query.

The consequence if it is wrong. A refrigeration controller does not hold data worth stealing. It sets temperature, defrost cycles and alarm thresholds, and the loss event is spoiled stock, a food safety incident, and - at scale, across a national grocery estate in the run-up to Christmas - a supply disruption with no data breach anywhere in it. That is precisely the kind of incident the NCSC's own annual review warned about three weeks ago when it assessed AI-assisted attacks on critical national infrastructure as highly likely by 2028, and it is also the cheapest available retaliation against a soft UK target. It is worth reading this entry alongside the UK's public confirmation of offensive cyber operations against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea, reported on 20 November.

Confidence and caveats. Confidence is medium overall because no NCSC, Defra, FSA or RDM primary page was retrieved in this run - all direct fetches failed with DNS errors. Confidence is higher on the facts that recur across every outlet: the late-October discovery, Omega Solutions as discoverer, Pen Test Partners as verifier, the NCSC/Defra/FSA coordination, the three-week timeframe, thousands of controllers and tens of thousands of units, manual temperature monitoring at some sites, RDM shipping initial updates while disputing severity, and the NCSC's three-point advice. There is no CVE identifier. Device counts vary between 'thousands of controllers' and 'tens of thousands of fridges', which are different measures of the same estate and should not be added together. The discovering consultancy's name appears as both 'Omega Solutions' and 'Omega Systems' across outlets. No supermarket is named, and the total number of exposed controllers in the UK or abroad remains unknown.
recommended_actions: Ask your refrigeration contractor, in writing, whether any controller they have installed or maintain for you is reachable from the internet, and keep the answer. If you are in convenience retail, wholesale, hospitality, catering, pharmacy or vaccine cold chain, or food manufacturing, you were almost certainly not in the government programme.

Do not rely on your IT asset inventory to answer that question. These devices are commissioned by refrigeration contractors and typically never enter the inventory. Scan your own external address space instead, and look for web interfaces and controller banners on non-standard ports.
Apply RDM's security updates. They are described as initial, so track the vendor for follow-on releases rather than closing the ticket after the first one.

Change default credentials on every refrigeration, building management and environmental controller you own, not just the RDM units. The flaw class here is weak or default passwords, and it is not specific to one vendor - the same class was abused against Danfoss equipment in Europe.

Put the controllers behind a VPN or a dedicated management network and remove them from direct internet exposure. The NCSC's advice is explicit on this point and it is the control that survives the next vulnerability in the same device.

Extend the same question to every other contractor-installed connected device on your sites: building management, HVAC, CCTV, door entry, lighting, energy metering, vending. The refrigeration controllers are an instance of a general gap, which is that contractor-commissioned equipment is not in anyone's asset register.

Add a temperature-excursion alerting path that does not depend on the controller itself, and test it. If the controller is the thing under attack, the controller's own alarm is not a reliable witness.

For food businesses: brief your HACCP or food safety lead that a cyber incident is now a credible route to a temperature excursion, and make sure your food safety incident procedure includes a manual monitoring fallback. Staff at some sites in the government programme were checking temperatures by hand.

If you operate critical cold chain - pharmacy, vaccine storage, pathology, clinical samples - treat this as a resilience item at board level rather than an IT ticket, and record whether you have a tested manual fallback.

kql.name: Inbound access to refrigeration and building controller web interfaces
kql.description: Detects external reach to OT controller management ports. Replace the controller subnet list with your own site OT ranges. This is the detection that matters because exposure, not exploitation, is the finding.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
let otSubnets = dynamic(["10.50.", "10.60.", "192.168.90."]);  // replace with your OT / plant ranges
let controllerPorts = dynamic([80, 443, 8080, 8081, 8443, 502, 1911, 4911, 47808]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DestinationPort in (controllerPorts)
| where DestinationIP has_any (otSubnets)
| extend External = not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| where External
| summarize Attempts = count(), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort, 10), Devices = dcount(DestinationIP), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
    by SourceIP
| order by Attempts desc

kql.name: Authentication failures then success against OT controllers - weak password abuse

let lookback = 90d;

vulnerabilities.title: N-able Confirmed a Cyberattack Behind the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Outage After Three Days of Blaming 'Platform Configuration' - a Second, Separate Incident Has N-central Hosted Platforms Offline Worldwide and On-Premises Customers Told to Keep Servers Shut Down
affected_products: N-able Mail Assure - Hosted Cloud, all regions; disruption began 16 November 2026
N-able SpamExperts - Hosted Cloud, all regions; same incident
Affected sub-services: logging, mailbox synchronisation, management portal and quarantine (mail flow and filtering reported as unaffected)
N-able N-central hosted environments - taken offline across the Americas, Europe and Asia-Pacific (separate incident, per N-able)
N-able N-central on-premises - customers instructed to shut servers down and leave them off until N-able advises otherwise
Trigger for the N-central action: public release of 33 unpatched flaws with working exploit code, reported under the name 'Able2Shell'
vulnerabilities.summary:
This is the UK corporate item with the widest blast radius, because almost nobody affected by it is an N-able customer. They are customers of a managed service provider that is, and the control plane in question manages their endpoints.

Incident one, and the new fact in this window. N-able's Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud services suffered a multi-day disruption across all regions beginning 16 November. For the first two days N-able attributed it to 'a combination of platform configuration and service dependencies'. On 18 November the company confirmed the cause was a cyberattack in which one of its servers was compromised, and SecurityWeek's reporting on 20 November is what brought the confirmation to wider attention. N-able states it has found no evidence that customer data was compromised, and that the intrusion was unrelated to the separate N-central hosted outage. Mail flow and filtering continued; what went offline was logging, mailbox synchronisation, the management portal and quarantine. At least one outlet reports that credentials may have been stolen.

Read the attribution sequence, not just the outcome. A vendor told its customers for two days that a platform-wide outage was a configuration and dependency problem, then said it was an intrusion. That is not necessarily bad faith - early incident attribution is genuinely hard, and 'configuration' is what a compromised server often looks like from the outside. But for a customer it means the first supplier statement in an outage is a hypothesis, not a finding, and your own incident decisions should not be anchored to it. If you stood down an internal investigation on 16 or 17 November because your supplier said it was a configuration issue, reopen it.

Why quarantine and logging being offline matters more than it sounds. Those are precisely the components you would need in order to investigate a phishing wave during the outage. Mail continued to flow and filter while the ability to review what was quarantined, synchronise mailboxes and read the logs was unavailable. Any organisation whose email security sat behind Mail Assure or SpamExperts between 16 and 20 November has a gap in its email forensic record for that period, and should treat that gap as a known limitation rather than as an absence of events.

Incident two, which is the supply chain problem. Separately, a researcher publicly released 33 unpatched flaws in N-central - the remote monitoring and management tool many MSPs use to run their clients' computers - with working exploit code, reported under the name Able2Shell. N-able declared a critical security incident, took hosted N-central environments offline across the Americas, Europe and Asia-Pacific, and told on-premises customers to shut their servers down and leave them off until advised otherwise. The practical effect for an MSP is that the console used to manage every customer endpoint went dark, and for the MSP's customers it means patching, monitoring and remote support for their estate stopped. This feed recorded on 20 November that N-able had shipped HF3, permanently removing the Legacy API and patching 17 further zero-days; today's sources describe hosted environments still offline and MSPs awaiting a hotfix, and do not agree on the restoration state. The discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved - confirm the current status with your MSP directly, because that is the only authoritative answer for your estate.

What a UK organisation should actually do. The useful question is not about N-able. It is: who can reach my endpoints with SYSTEM-level privilege, through what tool, and what happens to my security posture when that tool is switched off? Most UK mid-market and public sector bodies that outsource IT cannot answer that from their own records, and an RMM agent is the highest-privilege software on the estate. Ask the MSP in writing: do you use N-central or Mail Assure; was your instance affected; is it back; what are you doing to validate that agents were not abused while the console was down; and what is our forensic coverage for the outage period. Get the answer in writing because it is also your Article 28 processor assurance record.

Confidence and caveats. Confidence is medium. High on the existence of both incidents, the 16 November start date, the initial configuration explanation, the 18 November cyberattack confirmation, the sub-services affected, N-able's statement of no evidence of customer data compromise, the public release of 33 N-central flaws with exploit code, and the instruction to shut down on-premises servers - these recur across SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Cyberpress, Windows Forum and vendor analyses. Low on the credential-theft claim, which appears in only one account. Some vendor blogs cite CVE-2026-125883 for the N-central flaws, but Huntress-sourced material states no CVE identifiers have been assigned - treat that CVE as unverified. The current restoration state of hosted N-central is genuinely unclear and conflicts with this feed's own 20 November entry. A ChannelDive article describing an 'N-able RMM platform breach' refers to a July release and appears to be a separate, older matter.
recommended_actions: Ask your managed service provider in writing today whether they use N-able N-central or Mail Assure/SpamExperts, whether their instance was affected, whether it is restored, and what they have done to validate that RMM agents on your estate were not abused while the console was offline. Keep the reply - it is also your processor assurance record.

If your email security ran through Mail Assure or SpamExperts between 16 and 20 November, record a known gap in your email forensic coverage for that period. Logging, mailbox synchronisation, management portal and quarantine were offline while mail continued to flow, so an absence of alerts for those days is not evidence of an absence of events.
If you stood down an internal investigation during 16-17 November on the basis that your supplier called it a configuration issue, reopen it. The cause was later confirmed as an intrusion.

Rotate credentials and API tokens used to integrate with Mail Assure/SpamExperts, and any credentials your MSP holds for your tenant. One account reports possible credential theft; rotation is cheap and the claim does not need to be confirmed first.

Inventory every tool that holds SYSTEM-level or equivalent privilege on your endpoints - RMM, patch management, backup agents, remote support - and record who operates it, how it authenticates, and what your monitoring and patching posture is when it is unavailable. This is the durable finding, not the N-able specifics.

Require multi-factor authentication and IP restriction on your MSP's access to your tenant, and audit the MSP's accounts in your directory for privilege they no longer need. An RMM compromise reaches you through those accounts.

Hunt retrospectively for anomalous RMM agent activity on your endpoints over the last 30 days: unexpected script execution, unexpected software deployment, and agent-initiated process creation outside maintenance windows.

Do not treat a vendor hotfix announcement as confirmation that your instance is patched and online. This feed's own 20 November entry recorded HF3 shipping, while today's sources describe hosted environments still offline. Ask your MSP for your instance's state, in writing.

If you are an MSP: assume your N-central console was reachable by anyone who read the public disclosure, and treat validation of agent integrity across every managed estate as the first task after restoration, ahead of resuming routine patching.

kql.name: RMM agent spawning scripting engines or remote tooling
kql.description: Primary detection for abuse of a managed RMM agent. An RMM agent legitimately runs scripts, so tune to your MSP's known maintenance windows and script set rather than alerting on all of it.
kql.query:
let lookback = 45d;
let rmmProcesses = dynamic(["nablermm.exe", "ncentral", "agent.exe", "BASupSrvc.exe", "winagent.exe", "takecontrol"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any (rmmProcesses)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cmd.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "rundll32.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| extend Hour = datetime_part("Hour", Timestamp)
| project Timestamp, Hour, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Encoded or download-and-execute commands via RMM
kql.description: Narrows the above to the commands that matter: encoded payloads, downloads and execution-policy bypass driven through the management agent.
kql.query:
let lookback = 45d;
let rmmProcesses = dynamic(["nablermm.exe", "ncentral", "agent.exe", "BASupSrvc.exe", "winagent.exe", "takecontrol"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any (rmmProcesses)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-enc", "-EncodedCommand", "FromBase64String", "DownloadString", "Invoke-WebRequest", "iwr ", "curl ", "-ExecutionPolicy Bypass", "-nop -w hidden")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Managed service provider account sign-ins from new locations
kql.description: An RMM compromise reaches you through the MSP's accounts in your tenant. Replace the domain filter with your MSP's identity domain or guest UPN pattern.
kql.query:
let lookback = 45d;
let baseline = 90d;
let mspPattern = "msp";  // replace with your MSP's identity domain fragment or #EXT# guest pattern
let known = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(baseline) .. ago(lookback))
    | where UserPrincipalName has mspPattern
    | summarize by IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where UserPrincipalName has mspPattern
| where IPAddress !in (known)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion), AppDisplayName, ResultType, ResultDescription
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Privilege and application consent changes by external or MSP identities
kql.description: Detects an MSP identity being used to grant itself or an application additional privilege in your tenant - the escalation step after an RMM compromise.
kql.query:
let lookback = 45d;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where OperationName has_any ("Add member to role", "Add app role assignment", "Consent to application", "Add service principal", "Add owner to application", "Update application")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| where Actor has_any ("#EXT#", "msp")  // tune to your MSP identity pattern
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, OperationName, Result, TargetResources
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vulnerabilities.title: UK Government Regulation: the FCA, PRA and Bank of England Cyber Resilience Guidance Consultation (GC26/9 / CP17/26) Is Confirmed as Published on 19 November and Aligned to the NCSC's Cyber Assessment Framework, With a Separate Bank of England Paper on AI and Quantum - Responses Due 26 February 2027
vulnerabilities.vendor: Financial Conduct Authority / Prudential Regulation Authority / Bank of England
affected_products: FCA Guidance Consultation GC26/9 and PRA Consultation Paper CP17/26 - cyber risk and resilience management
In scope: banks, insurers, financial market infrastructures, and FCA-regulated firms subject to the SYSC 15A operational resilience requirements
Out of scope but encouraged to refer to it: credit unions and several other categories
Separate Bank of England publication on AI and quantum effective practices, including the implications of quantum computing for public-key cryptography
Consultation closes 26 February 2027
vulnerabilities.summary:
Retained from yesterday at a lower rank because the window contains corroboration and correction rather than a new event, and both are worth recording.

The correction first. This feed carried the publication date as inside the 19-20 November window; the primary date is now confirmed as 19 November 2026, and Computer Weekly's 20 November coverage ('FCA lines up new cyber guidance for UK financial services sector') is secondary reporting of it rather than a fresh announcement. The documents are FCA Guidance Consultation GC26/9 and PRA Consultation Paper CP17/26, issued jointly, with a separate Bank of England publication on AI and quantum effective practices.

What it is, stated precisely, because the framing matters for how firms should respond. The regulators are explicit that this does not introduce new rules. It is guidance that, once finalised, they will use when supervising and enforcing compliance with rules that already exist. Firms sometimes read 'no new rules' as 'no action required'. The opposite is closer to the truth: guidance of this kind tells you the standard against which your existing obligations will be judged, which makes it more immediately operative than a new rule subject to an implementation period. The content covers how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from cyber risks and incidents.

The detail with the most practical consequence. The guidance aligns with recognised cyber frameworks, and the NCSC's Cyber Assessment Framework is named among them. That is the item to act on this week, because it means a UK financial services firm can anticipate the supervisory yardstick by self-assessing against the CAF now, before responding to the consultation. It also quietly extends the CAF's reach: a framework built for critical national infrastructure is becoming the reference point for financial services supervision, which is a reasonable expectation for public bodies to apply to their own suppliers too.

Scope, which firms will get wrong. In scope: banks, insurers, financial market infrastructures, and FCA-regulated firms subject to the SYSC 15A operational resilience requirements. Credit unions and several other categories are excluded, but are encouraged to refer to the guidance anyway - and an excluded firm that ignores it will still find the guidance shaping what a supervisor considers reasonable under the rules that do apply to it.

Why now. October 2026 was the second-highest month for cyber incidents reported to the FCA in five years. That figure, alongside the ICO's record Q3 cyber report volumes recorded in this feed on 20 November, is the evidence base the regulators are acting on. It is also a useful sanity check on the rest of this report: the items at ranks 1, 3 and 5 are exactly the kind of third-party and management-plane exposures that drive those numbers.

The quantum half, which nobody will prioritise and which has the longest lead time. The Bank of England's separate publication on AI and quantum effective practices includes the implications of quantum computing for public-key cryptography. The honest assessment is that no UK firm will act on this in the next quarter, and that the firms which eventually find it painless will be the ones that started their cryptographic inventory - what algorithms, in what systems, with what certificate lifetimes, under whose ownership - in 2026 rather than in 2029. That inventory is also useful immediately for entirely non-quantum reasons, which is the argument for starting it.

Confidence and caveats. Confidence is high on the 19 November publication date, the document references GC26/9 and CP17/26, the joint FCA/PRA/BoE authorship, the 'no new rules' characterisation, the scope including SYSC 15A firms and excluding credit unions, the CAF alignment, the separate AI and quantum publication, the October 2026 incident statistic and the 26 February 2027 response deadline - these are corroborated across the FCA press release listing, the Bank of England news listing, Regulation Tomorrow, beinsure, ITV News, The Paypers and Crowdfund Insider. No primary document text was retrieved in this run; all direct page fetches failed. The named-senior-manager expectation reported in this feed on 20 November remains single-source from one commentator summarising the draft and should be confirmed against Annex 1 before any firm acts on it.
recommended_actions: Self-assess against the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework now, and do not wait for the guidance to be finalised. The CAF is named as an aligned framework, which makes it the best available proxy for the supervisory yardstick.

Establish whether you are in scope. If you are an FCA-regulated firm subject to SYSC 15A, a bank, an insurer or a financial market infrastructure, you are. If you are a credit union or otherwise excluded, read it anyway - it will shape what a supervisor considers reasonable under the rules that do apply to you.
Do not read 'no new rules' as 'no action'. Guidance used in supervising and enforcing existing rules is operative immediately once finalised, with no implementation period to plan around.

Map the guidance's six functions - govern, identify, protect, detect, respond, recover - against your current control set and record the gaps with owners and dates. That gap register is also the raw material for your consultation response.
Diarise 26 February 2027 for the response and start now if you intend to argue any point. Consultation responses written in the final fortnight do not change outcomes.

Start a cryptographic inventory in response to the Bank of England's AI and quantum paper: which algorithms, in which systems, with what certificate lifetimes, under whose ownership. It is the long-lead item and it is immediately useful for ordinary certificate and cipher hygiene regardless of quantum timelines.

Feed your own third-party incident experience into the response. The regulators' stated trigger is rising reported incident volume, and this report's ranks 1, 3 and 5 are the management-plane and supplier exposures that generate it.

Public sector bodies outside financial services: use the CAF alignment as your own supplier assurance reference. Asking a supplier for a CAF self-assessment is now a mainstream request rather than an unusual one.

kql.name: Regulatory incident reporting clock - incidents by severity and age
kql.description: Supports the respond function and incident reporting obligations. Surfaces open incidents against their age so a reportable event is not discovered after the window has passed.
kql.query:
let lookback = 180d;
SecurityIncident
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, Status, Severity, Title, Owner) by IncidentNumber
| extend AgeHours = datetime_diff("hour", now(), TimeGenerated)
| where Status != "Closed"
| project IncidentNumber, Title, Severity, Status, Owner = tostring(Owner), AgeHours
| order by Severity asc, AgeHours desc

vulnerabilities.title: NGINX2Root: Censys Puts Roughly 9 Million NGINX Services on an Affected Version With HTTP/2 Enabled, Still No Confirmed In-the-Wild Exploitation and Still Not in KEV - but the Linux Kernel SCTP Flaw That Completes the Chain to Root Has No CVE and No Upstream Patch
affected_products: NGINX Open Source - fixed in 1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline)
NGINX Plus - fixed in 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1
NGINX Ingress Controller - upgrade to 5.8.0
F5 advisories K000163925 through K000163931, plus K000164058 for the out-of-band update, published 18 November 2026
Five CVEs collectively named 'NGINX2Root'; CVSS v4.0 9.2 (critical) / CVSS v3.1 8.1 (high) per F5
Unpatched second stage: a Linux kernel SCTP flaw used to escalate from the worker process to root - no CVE assigned and no upstream patch as at 19-20 November 2026
vulnerabilities.summary:
Held at rank 7 after yesterday's deliberate downgrade from rank 1, and the window supplies the numbers that justify keeping it there rather than higher - plus one detail that argues for keeping it on the list at all.

The exposure number. Censys reports approximately 9 million NGINX services running an affected version with HTTP/2 enabled. That is the largest reachable population in this report by two orders of magnitude, and it is the reason this cannot be dropped even with no confirmed exploitation. For comparison, the vCenter population at rank 1 is a fraction of that, but it is being actively exploited - which is the right way to read the two entries together. Population size sets the eventual cost; exploitation status sets this week's priority.

Exploitation status as at this window. The most recent reporting states no in-the-wild exploitation had been reported as of 19 November, and that CISA had not added the CVEs to KEV, per watchTowr. Public proof-of-concept code exists: Rapid7 and Censys have published PoCs, and the consistent characterisation is that the exploit is not plug-and-play. Sources genuinely conflict here - some say public exploit code is out, others say none has been released, and the latter appear to predate the PoC publications. Yesterday's assessment that a real attempt would be loud and rate-limitable - requiring on the order of 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic and a specific glibc memcpy build - stands unchallenged in this window.

The new reason to care, and it is a detection problem rather than a patching one. The HTTP/2 control frames this vulnerability class uses are not logged as requests. Your access logs will not show an attack, successful or otherwise. That is a far more serious property than the CVSS score, because it means the usual reassurance - 'we checked the logs and saw nothing' - is worthless here. The practical detection is the one Xint recommends: processes launched by the nginx worker user. If your nginx worker user has ever spawned a shell, an interpreter or a network client, you have your answer, and if you are not collecting process-creation telemetry from your web tier you cannot answer at all.

The part that remains unfixed. The chain to root runs through a Linux kernel SCTP flaw. As at 19-20 November it has no CVE identifier and no upstream patch, and Xint is withholding technical details until a fix is available. Patching NGINX therefore closes the entry point while leaving the escalation primitive in place for whatever reaches the worker process next. Two defensive consequences follow, and both are cheap: disable the SCTP kernel module where it is not needed - which on the overwhelming majority of UK web servers is everywhere - and make sure nginx workers run with the minimum privilege and a restricted filesystem view. Blacklisting an unused kernel module is a five-minute change that removes an unpatched escalation path, and it is the single highest-value action in this entry.

UK context. NHS England Digital issued its own cyber alert for the F5 NGINX vulnerabilities dated 19 November, recorded in this feed yesterday. The Cloud Security Alliance published a research note on the chain on 20 November. UK relevance is high simply because of how much of the UK public sector web estate sits behind NGINX, frequently as a reverse proxy in front of applications that are themselves the object of other entries in this report - which is why the Drupal installer deny rule recorded on 20 November and this patch belong in the same change ticket.

Naming, because it causes real confusion in change tickets. 'NGINX2Root' is not F5's or nginx.org's terminology, and some coverage refers to the HTTP/2 pair as 'nginx2shell'. Separately, this run could not confirm the CVE identifier CVE-2026-129182 against any source describing the five NGINX CVEs - it does not appear in any of the retrieved material. That identifier was recorded in this feed previously and should be treated as unverified until checked against F5's advisories; the authoritative mapping is in K000163925 through K000163931.

Confidence and caveats. Confidence is medium. High on the 18 November advisory date, the fixed versions across OSS, Plus and Ingress Controller, the dual CVSS scoring, the worker-crash-to-memory-corruption impact, the HTTP/2 control frames not being logged, the Censys 9-million figure, and the unpatched no-CVE SCTP kernel flaw. Conflicting on public exploit code availability, with the conflict most likely explained by publication timing. Unverified: the CVE-2026-129182 identifier, which appears in none of this run's sources. No F5 advisory, Censys dashboard or Xint write-up was retrieved directly.
recommended_actions: Patch NGINX Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, NGINX Plus to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, and NGINX Ingress Controller to 5.8.0. Verify the CVE-to-release mapping against F5 advisories K000163925 through K000163931 and K000164058 rather than against a scanner's identifier list.

Blacklist or disable the SCTP kernel module on every web server that does not need it, which is almost all of them. This is the highest-value action in this entry: the escalation stage of the chain is a kernel SCTP flaw with no CVE and no upstream patch, and removing the module removes the escalation path without waiting for a fix.

Do not conclude from your access logs that you were not attacked. The HTTP/2 control frames used here are not logged as requests. 'We checked the logs' is not a valid answer for this vulnerability class.

Hunt instead for processes launched by the nginx worker user over the last 60 days. Any shell, interpreter or network client spawned by that account is the detection. If you are not collecting process-creation telemetry from your web tier, that gap is the finding.

Confirm whether HTTP/2 is actually enabled on each affected service. Censys's 9 million figure is specifically services on an affected version with HTTP/2 on, and turning HTTP/2 off where it is not needed is a valid interim mitigation.

Rate-limit and cap HTTP/2 connection and frame volumes at the edge. The reported requirement of around 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic makes a genuine attempt loud, which only helps you if something is counting.
Review the privilege and filesystem view of the nginx worker process. The entry point gives code execution as the worker; everything after that depends on what the worker can reach.
Combine this change with the Drupal /core/install.php deny rule from this feed's 20 November entry if you run Drupal behind NGINX - same hosts, same window, same ticket.
NHS organisations: the NHS England Digital alert for these F5 NGINX vulnerabilities is dated 19 November. Action it through your normal process and record the response.
Correct your records if they carry CVE-2026-129182 for this issue. That identifier could not be confirmed against any source in this run; use F5's advisory numbers as the authoritative reference.

let lookback = 60d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where AccountName in~ ("nginx", "www-data", "nobody", "http", "apache")
| where FileName in~ ("sh", "bash", "dash", "python", "python3", "perl", "ruby", "php", "nc", "ncat", "socat", "curl", "wget", "base64", "chmod")

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("modprobe sctp", "insmod sctp", "sctp_", "setcap", "chmod u+s", "/etc/sudoers", "pkexec", "unshare -r")
    or (AccountName in~ ("nginx", "www-data", "nobody", "http") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sudo", "su -", "id -u", "capsh"))
