kql.description: A genuine attempt reportedly needs on the order of 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, which is loud if something counts it. Surfaces single sources with abnormal inbound byte volume to web services.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DestinationPort in (443, 8443)
| summarize TotalBytes = sum(toreal(coalesce(SentBytes, 0)) + toreal(coalesce(ReceivedBytes, 0))), Connections = count()
    by SourceIP, DestinationIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| extend GB = round(TotalBytes / 1073741824.0, 2)
| where GB > 5
| order by GB desc

kql.description: Post-exploitation callback detection. A reverse proxy should have a narrow, known egress profile; anything else on the list is worth explaining.

| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 10), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| order by Connections desc

vulnerabilities.title: The European Commission Confirmed an AI-Assisted Cyberattack That Took Its HR, Medical Reimbursement and Translation Systems Offline for More Than Ten Days - Detected 22 October, Confirmed Publicly Only on 19 November, With CERT-EU Reportedly Detecting the Use of a Publicly Available AI Tool Called ARTEX
affected_products: Sysper - the European Commission's HR platform
MyPMO - the Commission's medical reimbursement system
Commission translation systems
Personnel systems reported as affected for more than ten days; most services since restored
Reported tooling: ARTEX, described as a publicly available AI tool for finding weaknesses in IT systems
vulnerabilities.summary:
Not a UK incident, and included deliberately. Three weeks ago the NCSC's annual review assessed that attackers would highly likely use AI-powered malware in a ransomware attack on UK critical national infrastructure by 2028. This is the first public confirmation by a major European government body that an AI-assisted attack has already taken its internal systems down, and it is the closest available read on what that class of incident actually looks like when it lands on a large public administration.

What happened. The first signs were detected on 22 October 2026. Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed the incident publicly at a press briefing on Thursday 19 November, after Politico reported it. Affected services include Sysper, the Commission's HR platform, MyPMO, its medical reimbursement system, and its translation systems. Personnel systems were reported as unavailable for more than ten days. Most affected services have since been restored, though the full extent of the damage remains unclear. Regnier described it as an AI-generated cyber campaign involving a publicly available AI tool, which he did not name; Politico reported that CERT-EU detected the attackers using ARTEX, a publicly available AI tool for finding weaknesses in IT systems. No attribution to a known group has been made, and Regnier said he was not aware of any ransom demand.

The detail worth taking seriously, which is not the AI part. It is the four-week gap between detection on 22 October and public confirmation on 19 November, for an incident that took an HR system and a medical reimbursement system offline for over ten days. Staff of the affected organisation experienced a visible, prolonged outage of systems holding their employment and medical reimbursement data while the cause was not publicly stated. For any UK public body reading this, the transferable question is not 'could AI tooling be used against us' - assume yes - but 'what is our stated position on day three of a ten-day outage in a system holding staff medical data, and who decides it'. That is a communications and governance decision made under pressure, and it is better made in advance.

What the AI element does and does not mean. ARTEX, as described, is a publicly available tool for finding weaknesses in IT systems. That is vulnerability discovery and reconnaissance acceleration, not autonomous attack. The practical effect is to compress the time between a weakness existing and someone finding it, and to widen the set of people capable of finding it. It does not introduce a new vulnerability class, and it does not need a new control: the defence is the same hygiene, applied faster. The realistic consequence is that the grace period between a vulnerability becoming known and being probed at scale shrinks - which is exactly the pattern visible at ranks 1, 3 and 7 of this report, and precisely what the NCSC's annual review told UK organisations to plan for when it urged them to prepare for a rush of security updates.

UK relevance, concretely. UK central government, devolved administrations and arm's-length bodies run the same classes of system as the ones hit - HR platforms, occupational health and reimbursement systems, translation services - usually from SaaS suppliers, often with the same supplier serving many bodies. Those systems are rarely on the critical-systems list because they are not service-delivery systems, which means they attract less monitoring and longer patch windows while holding staff personal and medical data. The ten-day outage is the part to plan for.

Confidence and caveats. Confidence is medium. High on the 22 October detection date, the 19 November public confirmation by spokesperson Thomas Regnier, the affected systems Sysper, MyPMO and translation, the ten-day-plus duration, the absence of attribution and the absence of a known ransom demand - these are consistent across SecurityWeek, The Record, Help Net Security, Infosecurity Magazine and Brussels Times. Medium on the ARTEX identification, which is Politico's reporting of CERT-EU's detection and was not confirmed by the Commission's spokesperson, who declined to name the tool. Disputed on data impact: SecurityWeek reports no evidence of a data breach, while Infosecurity, citing Politico, reports that the attack may have breached employee personal information - both are recorded, unresolved. One source dates the confirmation to 26 October rather than 19 November, which conflicts with the majority account. No primary Commission or CERT-EU statement was retrieved in this run. The investigation remains open.
recommended_actions: Decide now what you would say on day three of a prolonged outage in a system holding staff personal or medical data, and who has authority to say it. The transferable lesson here is the four-week gap between detection and public confirmation, not the AI tooling.

Add HR, occupational health, payroll and reimbursement systems to your critical-systems list if they are not already on it. They hold staff personal and medical data, they are usually SaaS, and they typically attract less monitoring and longer patch windows than service-delivery systems precisely because they are not service-delivery systems.

Plan for a ten-day outage of those systems specifically, not just for a breach of them. Document the manual fallback for payroll, expenses, absence recording and medical reimbursement, and confirm somebody owns it.
Ask your HR and occupational health SaaS suppliers for their incident notification commitments in writing, including how quickly they will tell you the cause and not merely that there is an outage.

Shorten your own patch cycle for internet-facing systems rather than adding an AI-specific control. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery compresses the time between a weakness existing and someone finding it; it does not create a new vulnerability class. The defence is existing hygiene applied faster.

Re-read the NCSC's November annual review guidance to plan for a rush of security updates, and check that your emergency change process can actually absorb several out-of-cycle criticals in one week. This report alone contains four.

Monitor for automated, broad reconnaissance against your external estate - high-rate, wide-surface, low-noise scanning - as a standing signal rather than a one-off hunt. That is what tooling of this class produces.

Do not record this as an AI incident in your risk register and leave it there. Record it as a prolonged outage of staff-data systems with delayed cause attribution, because that is the risk you can actually manage.

Boutinot Limited (UK wine importer) - Aurora leak-site post dated 19 November 2026; approximately 384 GB claimed from a corporate file server

Halfords Group plc - N0n listing; RedPacket Security dates the post 9 November while Ransomware.live logged it 20 November; RedPacket warns N0N listings have included unverified or fabricated victim claims
Audio Note UK Ltd (high-end audio manufacturer) - Osiris leak-site claim, 11 November 2026, unconfirmed
Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase - customer data published by N0n, obtained from unnamed third-party service providers rather than the companies' own systems
Nvidia - named by The Gentlemen; Nvidia investigating a possible third-party partner incident and reports no indication its own systems or networks were affected
vulnerabilities.summary:
This entry consolidates the UK corporate extortion picture in the window and is deliberately marked low confidence throughout. Every item in it is a criminal group's claim on a leak site. None has a victim statement confirming it, and one of the groups involved has a documented record of publishing claims that do not hold up. Read it as a watchlist, not as a list of breaches.

The largest and most sensitive UK claim. Ransomware.live logged an Aurora claim against William Cook Holdings Limited, the Sheffield-based industrial castings group, on 20 November. The claimed dataset is 1.1 TB exfiltrated from a file server at the Stanhope site, said to include employee personal data and payroll records. If accurate, the sensitive element is the employee data rather than the volume: payroll records carry names, addresses, national insurance numbers, bank details and salary, which is the combination that enables both identity fraud and convincing payroll-diversion approaches to the employer itself. There is no company statement.

The second Aurora claim. Aurora posted a claim against Boutinot Limited, the UK wine importer, on 19 November, asserting approximately 384 GB taken from a corporate file server. The post describes data theft and does not state whether systems were encrypted. Two UK manufacturing and distribution businesses claimed by the same group within 48 hours is the pattern worth noting - it suggests either a shared access route, a shared supplier, or simply that Aurora is working a UK mid-market seam. Nothing in the reporting distinguishes between those.

The one to be most careful with. Halfords Group plc appears on an N0n listing. The dates do not agree: RedPacket Security dates the post 9 November, Ransomware.live logged it on 20 November. More importantly, RedPacket explicitly warns that listings attributed to N0N have included unverified or fabricated victim claims and advises treating the post as unconfirmed. This feed recorded the same caution about N0n's UK retail listings on 20 November and downgraded them to a low-confidence note; that assessment is retained. Do not brief a board on a Halfords breach on this evidence.

And yet N0n has now published something substantive. The same group claimed responsibility for publishing customer data belonging to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase - obtained, all three companies say, from third-party service providers rather than from their own systems. The responses are notably measured and worth reading as a template. Visa says the incident involved a third-party service provider in the Asia-Pacific region and that card numbers were not affected. Mastercard acknowledges exposure of a limited quantity of email addresses - non-payment information - from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit programme. JPMorgan says attackers accessed marketing data that could include customer names and email addresses. None of the three named the third parties. Cybernews notes the published records may be test data and that the origin and authenticity have not been independently verified. The analytic point: a group with a record of fabricated claims has also produced a real third-party incident, which means the correct posture toward N0n is neither dismissal nor acceptance but verification, case by case.

The lesson the financial-sector response actually teaches. Three of the largest payment and banking brands in the world were exposed through suppliers and none of them would name the supplier. For a UK organisation that is not a reassurance, it is a warning about your own position: if a shared marketing, benefits or loyalty platform is breached, you will learn about it from a leak site, your public statement will be constrained by what the supplier will let you say, and your customers will not accept 'a third party' as an answer. The control is knowing, now, which suppliers hold your customer contact data and what your notification obligations and communications position are for each.

Nvidia, for completeness. Nvidia is investigating a possible third-party partner incident after The Gentlemen named it as a victim. Nvidia says it has no indication its own systems or networks were affected, and the group has neither published files nor identified the data it claims to hold, leaving the claim unsubstantiated. The Gentlemen is among the highest-volume groups of 2026 by leak-site count, and high volume plus unsubstantiated naming is a known pattern for pressure-building.

Context on the counts, since they will be quoted at you. Qilin leads UK leak-site claims in 2026 at 73 published claims, ahead of The Gentlemen at 49, DragonForce at 26 and Akira at 15, on one tally. A separate H1 2026 analysis counts up to 37 British organisations, which means the two sources define 'UK victim' differently. Overall, Qilin has around 1,165 listings or 12.1% of all 2026 leak-site victims as at 11 November, with The Gentlemen at 1,084 and Akira at 439. Treat all of these as claim counts, not breach counts - Bitdefender itself notes it cannot independently verify them.

Confidence and caveats. Confidence is low by design. The leak-site claims are corroborated only in the sense that multiple trackers logged the same posts; no victim statement confirms any UK claim in this entry. The Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan statements are the one well-sourced element and are reported consistently across several outlets. Dates for the Halfords listing conflict between trackers. No link between the N0n financial-sector leak and the SitusAMC breach was established in any source, despite the two being adjacent in coverage - do not merge them. No primary leak-site content was examined in this run and no direct page fetch succeeded.
recommended_actions: Do not brief anyone on these as confirmed breaches. Every UK item here is an unverified criminal claim, and one of the groups involved has a documented record of fabricated listings. Record them as monitoring items with named owners and a review date.

If you are a supplier to, customer of, or in the same group as William Cook Holdings or Boutinot: treat the claims as a prompt to check your own shared-access paths, shared file transfer, and any credentials either organisation holds for you.

William Cook Holdings specifically - if the payroll claim is accurate, the follow-on risk is payroll-diversion fraud against the employer and identity fraud against staff. Any organisation that processes payroll changes on the strength of an email should treat employee bank detail changes as requiring out-of-band verification, which is good practice regardless of this claim.

Identify today which of your suppliers hold your customer contact data - marketing platforms, benefits and loyalty programmes, mailing houses, CRM integrators - and record your notification obligation and communications position for each. The Visa/Mastercard/JPMorgan pattern is that you learn from a leak site and then cannot name the supplier.

Decide in advance what you will say when the breached party is a third party you cannot name. All three financial institutions here gave minimal, carefully scoped statements, and their customers still had to accept 'a third party' as the answer. Draft yours before you need it.

Monitor leak sites for your own organisation, your parent, your subsidiaries and your major suppliers, and route hits to a named owner rather than to a mailbox. A listing is often the first notification a UK organisation receives.

Treat any N0n listing as requiring independent verification before action, in either direction. The group has produced both fabricated claims and a substantive third-party financial-sector leak in the same month.

Use claim counts as trend data only. Qilin leads UK leak-site claims in 2026; the trackers disagree on totals because they define 'UK victim' differently, and none of the counts are confirmed breaches.
Do not link the N0n financial-sector leak to the SitusAMC breach. No source established a connection, and the two appear adjacent in coverage only.

vulnerabilities.title: Deadline and Patch-Completeness Board as at 21 November 2026: Apache Axis, REDCap, LiteLLM and Synology KEV Deadlines Fall Today With No Vendor Fix at All for Axis - and phpAfterShell CVE-2026-126714 Is Still Not in KEV While Public PoC Availability Is Disputed
affected_products: Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436 (unsafe reflection) - KEV dateAdded 2026-11-18 per the catalogue; no vendor fix available at all
Vanderbilt REDCap CVE-2026-90817 (code injection) - KEV dateAdded 2026-11-18 per the catalogue
BerriAI LiteLLM CVE-2026-40217 (unprotected alternate channel) - KEV dateAdded 2026-11-18 per the catalogue
Synology DiskStation Manager CVE-2024-10441 (improper encoding or escaping of output) - KEV dateAdded 2026-11-18 per the catalogue
PHP - phpAfterShell CVE-2026-126714, session-file corruption to RCE in the default file-based session handler; fixed in 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 and 8.6.0
PHP CVE-2026-129481 - listed by PHP as an INCOMPLETE FIX for CVE-2026-109619 (PHP2Shell), the confirmed initial-access leg of in-the-wild attacks on Check Point gateways
Shadowserver flagged CVE-2025-11141 as confirmed exploited on 19 November 2026
vulnerabilities.summary:
The housekeeping entry, and it carries the governance finding this feed now considers its most important recurring theme.

Deadlines falling today. Four KEV entries reach their remediation deadline on 21 November: Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436 (unsafe reflection), Vanderbilt REDCap CVE-2026-90817 (code injection), BerriAI LiteLLM CVE-2026-40217 (unprotected alternate channel) and Synology DiskStation Manager CVE-2024-10441 (improper encoding or escaping of output). A dating discrepancy is worth recording: SC World reported this group as added on 20 November, while the catalogue dates them 18 November, with deadlines of 21 November or 2 December depending on the entry. The catalogue date is the one to work from.

The one with no fix. Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436 has no vendor fix available at all. A KEV deadline against a vulnerability with no patch means the only available remediation is removal, isolation or replacement, and the deadline arriving today does not change that. Axis appears in UK estates mostly as an embedded dependency inside older Java integration middleware rather than as a product anyone chose, which means the hard part is finding it. Search your build artefacts and deployed WAR/EAR files for axis jars rather than looking in your software inventory.

The UK relevance of REDCap, which is easy to miss. REDCap is research data capture software, widely deployed across UK universities, NHS research units and clinical trial teams, and it holds research participant data including health data. It is also frequently operated by a research group rather than by central IT, which means it may not be in the patch pipeline at all and may not have an owner who reads KEV. If your institution does research, someone needs to ask the question today.

The patch-completeness finding, which is the real content of this entry. Three cases are now live simultaneously. PHP lists CVE-2026-129481 as an INCOMPLETE FIX for CVE-2026-109619 - PHP2Shell, already confirmed as the initial-access leg of in-the-wild attacks on Check Point gateways. Apache Roller's CVE-2026-129448 is the same bug as CVE-2026-82384, patched in September for 6.1.5 only and now confirmed exploited (rank 3). And Cisco Expressway X15.5.20 reportedly fixes CVE-2026-76466 while leaving PHP2Shell open (also rank 3). Add the Zyxel wrong-KEV-CVE case from earlier this month and that is four instances in three weeks where a correct remediation record describes an exposure that is still open. The operational consequence is specific and uncomfortable: an identifier-matching vulnerability scanner will agree with the wrong record, so neither your ticket nor your scanner can be trusted as evidence of closure on a reissued or incompletely fixed CVE. The only reliable check is the vendor's own release notes for the specific version you are running. This is worth raising at whatever forum owns vulnerability management in your organisation, because it is a process finding rather than a technical one.

phpAfterShell status. CVE-2026-126714 corrupts PHP session files to achieve remote code execution through the default file-based session handler, discovered by Depthfirst. As at 19-20 November, neither the PHP maintainers nor the researchers had reported attacks, and it is not in CISA's KEV catalogue. PoC availability is genuinely disputed: Italy's national CSIRT and the Ubuntu security tracker both state that proof-of-concept code is publicly available, while Wiz reports no observed exploitation and notes that six GitHub repositories merely naming the CVE do not prove a working exploit exists. Exploitation is not automatic - it requires file-based sessions, which is the PHP default, plus an exploitable gadget chain in the application's own code, which is not. The fix is PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0; where patching is delayed, setting session.upload_progress.enabled to 0 in php.ini closes the primary attack path and is a configuration change you can make this afternoon.

One additional exploitation signal from the window. Shadowserver flagged CVE-2025-11141 as confirmed exploited on 19 November, alongside a batch of older CVEs from 2017 through 2023 re-flagged on the same day. Old CVEs being actively re-exploited is the ordinary background condition of the internet and a useful reminder that this report's newest entries are not the only thing hitting your perimeter.

Confidence and caveats. Confidence is medium. High on the four KEV entries and their catalogue dateAdded of 18 November, the absence of any Apache Axis vendor fix, the PHP fixed versions, the php.ini mitigation, the requirement for file-based sessions plus a gadget chain, phpAfterShell's absence from KEV, and the PHP INCOMPLETE FIX relationship between CVE-2026-129481 and CVE-2026-109619. Disputed and recorded as such: public PoC availability for phpAfterShell. Conflicting: the KEV dateAdded for this group between SC World (20 November) and the catalogue (18 November), and the due dates between 21 November and 2 December by entry. CISA's catalogue pages could not be fetched directly in this run; the KEV listing used here came from an aggregated feed mirror. Verify your own deadline dates against the catalogue before using them in a compliance record.
recommended_actions: Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436 - accept that there is no patch and decide today between removal, network isolation and replacement. Find it by searching build artefacts and deployed WAR/EAR files for axis jars, not by looking in your software inventory; it is almost always an embedded dependency in older Java middleware rather than a product anyone installed.

REDCap CVE-2026-90817 - ask your research computing function, research governance lead or individual research groups today whether they run REDCap. It holds participant health data and is frequently operated outside central IT, so it may have no owner in your patch pipeline.

BerriAI LiteLLM CVE-2026-40217 and Synology DSM CVE-2024-10441 - confirm your versions and patch. LiteLLM in particular tends to appear in AI proof-of-concept deployments that were never formally onboarded, so check with whoever is experimenting rather than only with the asset database.

Raise patch completeness as a process item with whoever owns vulnerability management. Four cases in three weeks - PHP CVE-2026-129481 as an incomplete fix for PHP2Shell, Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448 reissuing CVE-2026-82384, Cisco X15.5.20 leaving PHP2Shell open, and the Zyxel wrong-KEV-CVE case - mean a closed ticket and a clean scanner result are no longer sufficient evidence of closure.

For any CVE marked as an incomplete fix or a reissued identifier, verify against the vendor's release notes for the exact version you run. Do not accept an identifier-matching scanner result, because it will agree with the wrong record.

Re-open any PHP remediation closed in October against CVE-2026-109619 and check it against CVE-2026-129481. PHP2Shell is a confirmed in-the-wild initial-access vector on Check Point gateways, so this is the highest-consequence of the incomplete-fix cases.

phpAfterShell CVE-2026-126714 - patch to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0. If the change window is further out, set session.upload_progress.enabled to 0 in php.ini today; it closes the primary attack path and takes minutes.

Check whether your PHP applications use file-based sessions, which is the default. Moving sessions to Redis or another non-file handler removes the precondition for this vulnerability class entirely and is worth considering as a standing hardening decision rather than a one-off fix.

Verify your own KEV deadline dates against CISA's catalogue rather than against press coverage. Secondary sources disagree on both the dateAdded and the due dates for this group, and a compliance record built on a press date is wrong.

Do not let the newest CVEs crowd out the old ones. Shadowserver re-flagged CVE-2025-11141 and a batch of 2017-2023 CVEs as actively exploited on 19 November; those are hitting your perimeter alongside everything at ranks 1 through 3.

summary_statistics.highest_priority_action: Six things, and the first two are the only ones that cannot wait for Monday. (1) TREAT VCENTER AS A COMPROMISE HUNT, NOT A PATCH. CVE-2026-123890 was exploited as a zero-day from early September until Broadcom shipped a fix on 19 November, by ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221), and CISA gave it a three-day KEV deadline of 23 November. Patching closes the door on an actor who may have been inside for ten weeks; it does not evict them. Enumerate every vCenter SSO administrator account against your change records, look for access to or copies of /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb, and decide this week whether to rotate SAML Security Token Service signing material - because an attacker holding it can mint valid assertions for everything that trusts your identity provider and no password reset revokes that. Scope the hunt to vCenter, ESXi and the adjacent Linux appliances, because the reported intrusion reached vCenter through appliances with no EDR coverage. If you are on the 7.0 branch, check Broadcom's matrix directly: one report states no public patch exists for that end-of-general-support line, which makes this an isolation decision rather than a patching one. NHS organisations: CC-4899 is already in your queue, dated 19 November. (2) IF YOU RUN APACHE ROLLER, DO NOT TRUST THE MITIGATION YOU PROBABLY APPLIED. Disabling XML-RPC in the Roller admin interface does NOT mitigate CVE-2026-129448, because affected versions deserialise the request before checking whether the feature is enabled. Upgrade to 6.1.6 or later, block POST requests to /roller-services/xmlrpc at the proxy, and specifically re-check anything you patched in September under CVE-2026-82384 - that release fixed 6.1.5 only and the same bug is now confirmed exploited. For Cisco Expressway, block TCP 4372 at the boundary today: the Erlang cookie is compiled into the software and identical on every install, so port reachability is the entire exposure. (3) BLACKLIST THE SCTP KERNEL MODULE ON YOUR WEB SERVERS. It takes five minutes and it removes the escalation stage of the NGINX2Root chain, which has no CVE and no upstream patch. While you are there, understand that this vulnerability class is invisible in access logs - the HTTP/2 control frames it uses are not logged as requests - so 'we checked the logs and saw nothing' is not an answer. The detection is processes spawned by the nginx worker user. Censys counts roughly 9 million affected services with HTTP/2 enabled. (4) ASK YOUR MSP, IN WRITING, WHETHER THEY RUN N-ABLE N-CENTRAL OR MAIL ASSURE, AND WHAT STATE IT IS IN. A researcher published 33 working exploits against N-central, N-able took hosted platforms offline worldwide and told on-premises customers to shut servers down, and separately confirmed that the Mail Assure and SpamExperts outage - initially blamed on 'platform configuration' for three days - was a cyberattack. If your email security ran through Mail Assure between 16 and 20 November, record a forensic coverage gap for those days: mail flowed while logging, quarantine and mailbox sync were offline, so an absence of alerts is not an absence of events. The durable question underneath this is the one worth answering properly: who can reach your endpoints with SYSTEM privilege, through what tool, and what happens to your security posture when that tool is switched off? (5) ASK YOUR REFRIGERATION AND BUILDING CONTRACTORS, IN WRITING, WHETHER ANY CONTROLLER THEY INSTALLED IS REACHABLE FROM THE INTERNET. RDM has now shipped initial security updates and the NCSC's guidance is explicit: apply them, change default credentials, keep the devices off the public internet. The government programme covered the major grocers. Convenience retail, wholesale, hospitality, catering, pharmacy and vaccine cold chain and food manufacturing were not covered, and most of them cannot answer this from their own records because a contractor commissioned the equipment and it never entered the IT asset inventory. Scan your own external address space rather than querying a database that was never going to contain the answer, and extend the same question to HVAC, CCTV, door entry and energy metering. (6) RAISE PATCH COMPLETENESS AT WHATEVER FORUM OWNS VULNERABILITY MANAGEMENT. Four cases are live at once: PHP lists CVE-2026-129481 as an INCOMPLETE FIX for PHP2Shell CVE-2026-109619, which is confirmed in-the-wild initial access on Check Point gateways; Apache Roller's new CVE is a reissue of a September fix that only covered 6.1.5; Cisco X15.5.20 reportedly closes CVE-2026-76466 but not PHP2Shell; and Zyxel published the wrong KEV CVE earlier this month. The consequence is not technical, it is evidential: an identifier-matching scanner agrees with a wrong remediation record, so neither your ticket nor your scan proves a bug is closed. Only the vendor's release notes for the exact version you run do that. And today's KEV deadlines - Apache Axis, REDCap, LiteLLM, Synology - include one with no vendor fix at all, so for Axis the decision is removal, isolation or replacement, and the search is in your build artefacts rather than your software inventory. If your institution does research, ask someone today whether a research group runs REDCap: it holds participant health data and it is usually outside central IT's patch pipeline.
